content: A drug allergy, also known as an immunologic drug reaction, is a specific type of adverse reaction to a medication that occurs due to activation of the immune system in response to the drug. Drug allergies are a subset of adverse drug reactions, which are broadly categorized into two types: Type A (predictable) and Type B (unpredictable). Drug allergies fall under the Type B category, along with pseudoallergic drug reactions. Drug allergies are classified based on two main criteria. The first classification, established by the World Allergy Organization, categorizes reactions based on the timing of onset—whether they occur within one hour of drug administration (immediate) or after one hour (delayed). The second classification is based on the type of immunologic reaction and the mediators involved. An allergic reaction to a drug does not occur upon the first exposure to the substance. The initial exposure allows the immune system to develop antibodies and memory lymphocytes specific to the antigen. However, drugs often contain multiple components, such as dyes, which can themselves act as allergens. This can lead to an allergic reaction even during the first administration of a drug if the patient has been previously sensitized to one of its components. For instance, a person allergic to a red dye will react to any new medication containing that dye. Drugs can trigger allergic reactions through various mechanisms, either by acting as direct antigenic particles or by activating immune cells through interaction with immune cell receptors. Certain types of drugs are more commonly associated with allergic reactions. Medications containing sulfa compounds, antibiotics, insulin, and iodinated drugs are frequent culprits. It is important to differentiate drug allergies from drug intolerances. A drug intolerance is a milder, non-immune-mediated reaction that does not require prior exposure to the drug. For example, many individuals who believe they are allergic to aspirin are actually experiencing a drug intolerance. Adverse drug reactions affect up to 10% of the global population and up to 20% of hospitalized patients. Among fatal cases of anaphylaxis, drugs are responsible for approximately 20% of deaths. Several risk factors increase the likelihood of developing a drug allergy. Patient-related factors include female gender, being young or middle-aged, genetic predisposition, certain viral infections (such as HIV or Epstein-Barr virus), and a history of atopy or previous drug allergies. Drug-related factors include high molecular weight compounds, intravenous or intramuscular administration, and frequent, prolonged, or high-dose exposure to the medication. Routine screening for drug allergies is generally discouraged, as it requires exposure to the drug, which could pose unnecessary risks of severe reactions. Screening may be considered in patients who require a specific medication and are at high risk for a severe allergic reaction. Testing is typically reserved for confirming a diagnosis in individuals who have already demonstrated an allergic reaction to a drug. In general, allergic reactions worsen with continued exposure to the offending agent. Symptoms of drug allergies can range from mild itching and rashes to severe exfoliative dermatologic conditions. Respiratory symptoms, such as wheezing and difficulty breathing, may also occur, and in severe cases, anaphylaxis and anaphylactic shock can develop. Physical examination findings in drug allergies vary widely depending on the specific manifestation and severity of the reaction. A thorough physical examination is essential to distinguish drug allergies from other conditions, with particular attention to the respiratory and cardiovascular systems to identify life-threatening reactions promptly. Drug allergy is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on patient history and physical examination. Laboratory findings during the acute phase of a reaction may provide supportive evidence but are not always specific. Skin testing and biopsies may be performed when the diagnosis is unclear. Management of drug allergies involves both acute and long-term treatment strategies. In cases where the offending drug is essential for treatment, desensitization protocols and graded challenges may be employed to allow the patient to tolerate the medication safely.
